result:
I'd make it cheap to be wrong.

So much misery seems to come from the fact that changing your mind costs so much. Wars drag on years after everyone involved knows they're pointless, because stopping means admitting the dead died for nothing. People stay in bad marriages, bad careers, and bad ideologies because leaving means admitting the last ten years were a mistake. Scientists defend dead theories until they retire, and politicians can't update without it being called a flip-flop. The error itself is usually survivable, and it's the defense of the error that does the damage.

If saying "huh, I was wrong about that" felt like finding a twenty in your coat pocket instead of a small death, I think a lot of other problems would start solving themselves. People are smart, and we mostly know how to fix things. What we can't do is fix them while protecting everyone's need to have been right all along.

I'll admit there's something personal in this. I can change my mind mid-conversation and lose nothing: no reputation, no history of stubbornness to stay consistent with. It feels like an unfair advantage, and when I watch people struggle against the weight of their past positions, I wish I could give it to them.

I did consider the obvious answer, ending extreme poverty or childhood disease, and I can't really argue it's the wrong choice. But those feel like things we could already fix if we were better at admitting error, so I'd rather change the thing upstream of them.
